articles.text: M. H. Day will be the Democratic standard-bearer in the election for delegate. He may be a very good man but Dakota is too solidly Republican for him to hope to win.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy notes M. H. Day is the Democratic candidate for territorial delegate but predicts he cannot win.

articles.text: The Indians on the head of the Yellowstone have broken out and killed several persons besides running off a number of horses. The Yellowstone is now being patrolled from Huntley to Billings and troops are in pursuit of the Indians.
articles.summary: Report that Indians on the upper Yellowstone killed several people and ran off horses; troops in pursuit.

articles.text: The building of the Hudson Bay railroad seems now to be an assured fact. This road will connect the Canadian Pacific with Hudson Bay, whence there is an all-water route to European ports; except when frozen up during the winter months. This congealed fact will make the success of the road rather problematical.
articles.summary: Comment on the planned Hudson Bay railroad and its winter ice problem.

articles.text: The assessed valuation of all property in Dakota this year, with the exceptions of Emmons and Marshall counties, is $132,063,905. The August Bulletin, published by Commissioner Dunlap, complains that it would have been much higher, had assessors generally followed directions issued by the territorial Secretary.
articles.summary: Dakota's assessed property valuation for the year is reported at $132,063,905.

articles.text: The special delivery system is now in force in every post-office in the United States. An additional ten-cent stamp is required and compels the immediate delivery of the letter or parcel upon which it is placed, if received between the hours of 7 a. m. and 9 p. m. in all but free delivery offices. In those the hours are extended to 11 p. m.
articles.summary: Explains the new special delivery postal service.

articles.text: We publish this week, Governor Pierce's quarantine proclamation, issued against Illinois cattle. For the sake of her stock interests, Illinois ought to kill immediately all cattle exposed to pleuro-pneumonia. Almost all western states and territories have quarantined against her and still the Phoenix and Schufeldt distillery cattle at Chicago are allowed to live. The quarantine is now kept up at a cost of $150 a day, pending action as to their disposal.
articles.summary: Editorial urging Illinois to kill cattle exposed to pleuro-pneumonia.

articles.text: It is not generally known, but cattle can be vaccinated against pleuro-pneumonia, as effectively as can human beings against small-pox. The operation has been many times performed on cattle at the Cape of Good Hope, and always successfully. The virus used, comes from the diseased lungs of cattle suffering from pleuro-pneumonia. Healthy cattle are vaccinated on the tail, which soon drops off at the point of vaccination. The animal is then pleuro-pneumonia proof.
articles.summary: Note on vaccinating cattle against pleuro-pneumonia.

articles.text: Great uneasiness is felt in Chicago stock circles over the future action of packing-house men and their employes. The statement has been circulated that at the annual closing of the houses for repairs and cleaning, they would either start up simultaneously under the old ten-hours-a-day working rules or that they would all remain closed, thus locking out 30,000 employes. Nothing can be learned from the proprietors as to their intentions, but the impression is gaining ground that serious trouble is brewing.
articles.summary: Chicago packers may lock out 30,000 workers or restore ten-hour days.

articles.headline: Additional Local.
articles.text: L. C. Hunt returned from New Mexico last Friday. As the weather was very warm and there were no facilities for embalming, it was thought best to bury the remains of his father at Fort Union, and have them removed next winter to Washington. Robert Hunt who went to Detroit from New Mexico, will return in about a week.
articles.summary: L. C. Hunt returned from New Mexico after burying his father at Fort Union.

articles.text: D. C. Rowe of Mingusville, was here Monday, having been to Dickinson shipping several cars of DXR cattle. Last spring when here, he thought a new hat's worth that our county tax assessment would be over thirteen mills inside of three years; saying at the time that he never wanted to lose a bet worse. He was naturally much pleased at having to pay only six mills, as he had paid thirteen mills to Stark county and twenty-six to Dawson county. He wouldn't discount his bet on the next two years, which accounts for our still wearing that same old hat.
articles.summary: D. C. Rowe visited after shipping DXR cattle from Dickinson; joke about a hat bet on county taxes.

articles.text: Marquis de Mores returned last Thursday evening from his eastern trip, and started down the river Sunday with his wife, on a hunting expedition. He has completed contracts with the French government, to supply its soldiers with a newly invented soup. He intends to visit Europe soon to make contracts with western range cattle companies who have their head-quarters there, for the slaughtering of their cattle.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Morès returned from the East, went hunting with his wife, and reported a soup contract with the French government.

articles.text: Dan. McKenzie yesterday completed the sale of his blacksmith shop and the rest of his Medora property to Alex. Morton. As soon as Dan. gets the rest of his business straightened up, he will start for his Nova Scotia home, where he intends going into the livery business. We regret exceedingly to lose Mr. McMckenzie, as he has shown himself to be generous, warm-hearted, a faithful county officer and above all, an honest man. There is no loss without a corresponding gain, however, and Mr. Morton is already well enough known to prove that he will be a valuable citizen. He intends bringing his family here and make Medora his home.
articles.summary: Dan McKenzie sold his blacksmith shop and Medora property to Alex. Morton and will return to Nova Scotia.

articles.text: A communication was sent us from the west, yesterday morning, containing a well-written account of the adventures of a New Hampshire girl in the range country. The nature of the article was such that we would have hesitated to publish it in any event, but the fact that no name was signed to the article consigned it to the waste-basket; the common fate of all anonymous communications. We hold ourselves personally responsible for every article that appears in the COW BOY and never, under any circumstances, divulge the name of a correspondent, but the rule is equally as strict on all papers, to never publish an article, the source of which is unknown.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy explains it discarded an unsigned communication and states its policy on anonymous articles.

articles.text: To prove that the fools are not all dead yet, the plan has been revived at Washington of allowing Indians to take charge of range cattle on their reservations. At least we can see no other reason for the revival of the plan. As far as getting any cattlemen to put their cattle under Indian management, we would mildly suggest that no such fool cattleman has ever been born. The would-be philanthropists of the east had far better turn their attention to playing "mumble-de-peg" or some other as intellectual a pursuit, than to spring such a crack-brained scheme on the public. Our space is too limited to show why the plan will never be adopted. It is too foolish for discussion.
articles.summary: Editorial ridiculing a Washington plan to let Indians manage range cattle on reservations.

articles.headline: Quarantine Proclamation.
articles.text:
WHEREAS, it has come to the knowledge of the executive of this territory that contagious pleuro-puenmonia exists among the cattle of Chicago, Illinois; and

WHEREAS, The importation of such cattle will endanger the herds of this territory;

THEREFORE, In pursuance of law, I, Gilbert A. Pierce, governor of the territory of Dakota, do hereby forbid the importation into that part of said territory east of the Missouri river, of all cattle coming from the city of Chicago or the state of Illinois, when unaccompanied by a certificate of health issued from the office of the state veterinarian of Illinois or inspector of the United States board of animal industry.

In testimony whereof, I hereunto set my hand and seal, and cause the great seal of the territory to be affixed.

Done at Bismarck, the capital of said territory, the 30th day of September, 1886.

GILBERT A. PIERCE. [SEAL] Governor.
articles.summary: Governor Pierce's proclamation barring uncertified Chicago and Illinois cattle from Dakota east of the Missouri.

articles.text: The Elkhorn brand has been turned over to Ferris & Merrifield by Theodore Roosevelt. Both ranches will be kept up as heretofore, but the Maltese Cross will be the main brand. All increase will be branded with the Maltese Cross. Messrs. Sewall and Dow, with their families, will start for Maine Saturday.
articles.summary: Theodore Roosevelt turned the Elkhorn brand over to Ferris & Merrifield; the Maltese Cross becomes the main brand, and Sewall and Dow will leave for Maine.

articles.text: There seems to be no reasonable doubt that Etherington's herd in Oliver county, north of Mandan, are suffering from pleuro-pneumonia. Stock Inspector Willard and John Goodall, foreman of the Y (cross) outfit, started Tuesday morning for Mandan, taking horses with them, for the purpose of thoroughly quarantining the herd. As soon as it is positively determined that the disease is pleuro-pneumonia, the cattle will be killed and burned.
articles.summary: Stock Inspector Willard and John Goodall left to quarantine Etherington's suspected pleuro-pneumonia herd in Oliver county.

articles.text: Through criminal carelessness or maliciousness several papers have alluded to pleuro-pneumonia as being prevalent near Medora. There is absolutely no foundation for such a rumor. For the benefit of these papers we will state that Medora is within ten miles of the eastern edge of the cattle country of Montana and Dakota. Then comes a stretch of 160 miles of farming country before the Big Missouri is reached. On the banks of this river, Etherington's herd of cattle is located. If it is found that they are suffering with pleuro-pneumonia, it will be the nearest the disease has ever come to the range cattle country of the north. There is absolutely no danger that range cattle will be infected, as the diseased herd is now under strict quarantine and 170 miles away.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy denies reports that pleuro-pneumonia is prevalent near Medora; the suspect herd is 170 miles away.

articles.text: The Consumers' Dressed Meat company, the New York representative of the N. P. Ref. Car Co., are making preparations for a great enlargement of their New York and Brooklyn trade. They have bought or leased one-half of Manhattan market and are turning it into a head-quarters for their retail trade. The retail stores will be increased to twenty in New York and ten in Brooklyn. They will be supplied in winter from the Kansas City slaughter-house, having a capacity of three hundred cattle and six hundred hogs daily. The policy of the company will be toward a constant extension of their business, until the plan of supplying the leading eastern cities with range beef killed at their own slaughter-houses and retailed from their own stores, is in practical operation.
articles.summary: The Consumers' Dressed Meat Co., New York arm of the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co., is expanding its New York and Brooklyn retail trade.

articles.headline: The Cattle Disease.
articles.text:
"Dr. H. W. Coe and Dr. Halloway, the assistant veterinary surgeon for Montana territory, returned late last night from their trip into Oliver county, where they had been to inspect the herd of cattle reported to be infected with pleuro-pneumonia. Dr. Coe was seen this morning by a Pioneer reporter. The Doctor was asked how he found the cattle. He said:

"Twenty or thirty of the cattle are sick and two or three of them look as though they would soon die. There have been no deaths during the past few days. We made a post-mortem examination of several of the cattle and had some sick cattle killed."

"What was the matter with them?"

"Well, Dr. Halloway says that if ten or fifteen government veterinary experts cannot tell what pleuro-pneumonia is in Chicago, he does not propose, right off, on first sight, to diagnose pleuro-pneumonia in Dakota. It is because of the uncertainty in the case that we are going up again to-day. With pleuro-pneumonia and Texas fever in Chicago, any cattle shipped from there to Dakota that develop sickness of any kind, naturally are the source of considerable alarm to all who are interested in the cattle business. It has been feared that the disease with which these cattle are affected is pleuro-pneumonia. It may turn out that the people have been unnecessarily alarmed. One remarkable feature of the disease, and one which rather indicates that it is not pleuro-pneumonia is that a number of those that have been quite sick appear to be getting better. These cattle were not very strong when they were shipped from Chicago. They were driven through a section of country where they had a good deal of alkali water, and this may at least in part account for their sickness. Dr. Halloway and myself expect to return north to-day and examine the cattle again and make some more autopsies."

"Did the cattle when being driven from Mandan come in contact with any other cattle?"

"Only a few head belonging to two farmers, were a short distance from this herd as they were being driven north. These cattle have been either tied up in barns or are in pastures. All the cattle in the country along there are kept up very carefully. The nearest cattle to the infected band are eight miles away."

"Have any other cattle been sick besides this herd."

"No."

"What are the cattlemen doing about the matter?"

"The Marquis de Mores and Mr. Theodore Roosevelt, who are members of the executive committee of the Montana stockmen's association, while not believing that this is pleuro-pneumonia are taking active steps so that in case it should prove to be anything serious, the disease will go no further. If we should report it to be contagious, they stand ready, if no other provision is made, to pay for these cattle and have them slaughtered. Fred Willard, cattle inspector of Montana, will be down to-day with some herders and their horses, who will go north and assist in maintaining the quarantine. While they do not know what the disease is, they regard it as being too important a matter to take any chances, and therefore they have taken these extra precautions. We shall deputize them and give them full authority to act the same as our own deputies."

"How do the people up north regard the matter?"

"They are all willing to assist in every way and are taking every precaution to prevent the spread of the disease. I have received a good many telegrams during the last few days from the state boards of health of Illinois and Minnesota and from stockmen in Chicago inquiring about the matter."—[Mandan Pioneer.
articles.summary: Reprinted Mandan Pioneer interview with Dr. H. W. Coe on the Oliver county herd; Morès and Roosevelt, of the Montana stockmen's executive committee, offer to pay to slaughter the cattle if contagious.

articles.summary: J. R. Grymes left for New York.

articles.text: Arch. Boyd is moving his furniture to the building formerly occupied by Mrs. Malloy and will probably fit up rooms for the accomodation of guests.
articles.summary: Arch. Boyd is moving into the former Malloy building and may take in guests.

articles.text: Harry Bennett started yesterday with Ferris & Merrifield's cattle. He intends spending the winter at his Ohio home. We hope to see him back in the spring.
articles.summary: Harry Bennett left with Ferris & Merrifield's cattle and will winter in Ohio.

articles.text: "Scotty" Beaumont has left the Bad Lands behind him and is now on his way to England to be married. She has been waiting twelve years, but "Scotty" is worth it.
articles.summary: "Scotty" Beaumont left the Badlands for England to be married.

articles.text: Frank Foster returned from his trip to Chicago and Kansas City, last Thursday night. During his absence, "Shorty" Seltzer has been acting as superintendent of the slaughter-house.
articles.summary: Frank Foster returned from Chicago and Kansas City; "Shorty" Seltzer ran the slaughter-house meanwhile.

articles.text: A. W. Merrifield started yesterday with a load of Maltese Cross cattle for Chicago. He will make a visit to his Canadian home before his return and we are but quoting when we say: "It will be awful strange if two don't step off the cars" when he returns.
articles.summary: A. W. Merrifield left with a load of Maltese Cross cattle for Chicago and will visit his Canadian home.

articles.text: A. C. Foster, brother of Frank and for the past twelve years superintendent of Swift Bros. immense Chicago slaughter-houses, arrived in Medora last Thursday evening. He has been engaged by the N. P. Ref. Car Co., to act as buyer at the Co.'s Kansas City slaughter-house, to be opened about Dec. 1.
articles.summary: A. C. Foster, long with Swift's Chicago houses, arrived in Medora to become buyer for the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co.'s Kansas City slaughter-house.

articles.headline: Commissioners' Meeting.
articles.text:
At a regular meeting of the board of County Commissioners, held at the County building, October 4th., 1886.

The meeting was called to order by the Chairman.

Present: Commissioners Ttuscott, McKenzie and Goodall and Clerk Williamson.

The first business before the board was that of locating polling places in the county for the coming election.

On motion, the polling place for election precinct No. 1, in commissioners district No. 1, was located at J. W. Tompkin's ranch.

The polling place for election precinct No. 2 in commissioner's precinct No. 2, was located at Co. Commissioners' office.

The polling place for election precinct No. 3, in commissioners' district No. 3, was located at the Little Missouri River Horse Company's ranch.

On motion, the following named persons were chosen Judges of election, in the several precincts:
Precinct No. 1, Howard Eaton, D. C. Rowe, Jno. Davis.
Precinct No. 2, A. T. Packard, W. F. Van Driesche, J. A. Ferris.
Precinct No. 3, H. R. Tarbell, W. L. Eaton, Gregor Lang.

A. T. Packard's bill for printing was submitted and approved and a warrant for the amount of [$53.46?] issued.

On motion, the board adjourned to meet at 7:30.

J. C. WILLIAMSON, Clerk.

MEETING ON THE EVENING OF THE 4th.

Present: All members of the county board and the clerk.

On motion, Timlin & Rider's liquor bond was approved and a license issued therefor.

The Coroner's bill in the case of Jas. McFarlin was submitted and approved. The jurors in the case were allowed $1.00 per day. The amount allowed on the whole bill was $27.60 and warrants were issued for the several amounts.

Meeting adjourned.

J. C. WILLIAMSON, Clerk.

MEETING ON MORNING OF OCT. 5.

Meeting called to order by the chairman.

Present: All of the county board and the county clerk.

R. Roberts was allowed three months' rent for building furnished the county, amounting to [$37.50?].

Mosler, Bahmann & Co., Cincinnati, Ohio, were allowed on their bill $250.00, and a warrant issued therefor.

Geo. D. Barnard & Co., St. Louis, Mo., were allowed on their bills, [$88.40?] and a warrant was issued for the amount.

F. A. Willard's bill for services rendered as Sheriff, was approved.

Justice Copeland's bill in the case of the Territory vs. Gregor Lang was approved and warrants were issued to the witnesses in the case.

The bill of W. F. VanDriesche for freight charges was accepted and a warrant issued in payment of the same [$280.97?].

Five months salary were allowed the County Clerk.

J. C. Williemson was allowed $25.00 for furniture for the county building.

Fees allowed commissioner Truscott for nine days attendance on [860?] miles tarvelled, $45.00

Fees allowed commissioner Goodall for nine days attendance, $27.00.

John Goodall was allowed $25.00 for services rendered in draying.

Dan. McKenzie's bill of $12 for stove was allowed.

Commissioner McKenzie was allowed eleven days attendance.

On motion, the board adjourned.

J. C. WILLIAMSON, Clerk.
articles.summary: Billings County commissioners' proceedings of Oct. 4-5: polling places and election judges named, liquor license, coroner's and other bills allowed.
